captions: Part nine. Running Actions well.
Cost, speed, debugging — and what else you can
automate.

First, cost. Public repositories on standard runners
are free.

Private repos get a monthly allowance of free
minutes
— two thousand on the Free plan, more on
paid plans.
Beyond that, you pay per minute. Linux is the

cheapest, Windows costs more, and macOS costs the
most.
One detail: each job is rounded up to a
whole minute. So twelve jobs of ten seconds bill
as twelve minutes, not two.
A giant matrix of tiny jobs can cost more
than you'd think.
Now speed. A slow pipeline is a tax on
every single change.
Start by caching dependencies.
Then split the work into parallel jobs.
For big builds, try a larger runner.

Stack those three, and an eighteen minute pipeline
can
drop to about five.
Path filters and cancel in progress go further —
they skip runs altogether.
Faster feedback means developers stay in flow.
Sooner or later, a run goes red. Here's how
to debug it.
Open the failed step. The error is usually in
the last few lines, and GitHub marks it with
an annotation.
Re-run just the failed jobs, instead of the whole
workflow.
Still stuck? Re-run with debug logging on, for much
more detail.
To iterate faster, the open source tool act runs
your workflows locally, in Docker.
And write to the job summary — a markdown
report right on the run page, for test results
and links.

Finally, remember: Actions is an automation
platform, not just
CI.
Teams use it to label and triage new issues,

close stale ones, and welcome first-time
contributors.
To generate release notes, and bump versions.
To run nightly scrapers, reports and backups.

And increasingly, to power AI. GitHub's own Copilot
coding
agent does its work inside an environment powered by
Actions.
If it happens on GitHub, you can probably automate
it.
Let's build two automations. First: auto-triage.
The trigger is issues, of type opened.
The job only needs permission to write issues.

We pass the issue number through an environment
variable
— the safe pattern from the security chapter —
along with the token that the gh command line
tool needs.
If the title mentions bug, add the bug label.
Then post a friendly first reply, so nobody waits
in silence.
Fifteen lines, and every new issue is triaged within
seconds.
Second: releases.
This workflow triggers on any tag that starts with
v.
Creating a release needs contents write permission.
It checks out the code, builds it, and zips
the output.

Then a single gh command creates the release,
attaches
the zip, and writes release notes from the merged
pull requests.
Now shipping a version is just: create a tag,
push it, done.
Issues, releases, schedules, chat ops — once you see
the pattern, you'll want to automate everything.
